pathway.title: DYCOM INDUSTRIES INC — Full credit assessment
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: - Scale and contracted visibility are the strongest supports. Contract revenues were USD 5,545.9 million in fiscal 2026 and backlog reached USD 12,242 million at August 1, 2026, with 86.6% of fiscal 2026 revenues under multi-year master service agreements, so earnings have a visible base even though customers are not committed to volumes. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 54–55; 10-K_2026-01-31_dy-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 49

- Leverage is moderate but not yet proven. Net debt over trailing reported EBITDA was 1.50x at January 2025, 2.99x at January 2026 and 2.73x at August 1, 2026, and 82.39% of drawn principal is secured term debt that ranks ahead of the 2029 notes. The trailing ratio holds acquired earnings for only part of the period, so the fall since year end is partly mechanical. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 19–21; calculation C05

- Cash interest cover of 10.49x flatters the position. Trailing cash interest holds the acquisition debt for only part of the year, and cash interest paid in the first half of fiscal 2027 annualised gives cover of 8.71x, against a covenant minimum of 2.50x that the company reports as met. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 21; calculation C02

- Free cash flow is the weakest dimension. Free cash flow was 61.84% of reported EBITDA in fiscal 2026, 24.28% in fiscal 2025 and negative in the first half of both fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2026, because receivables and seasonal working capital absorb cash before earnings convert. A supplier finance float of USD 367.4 million inside payables funds part of that cycle. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 29

- Liquidity is adequate but is being spent. Liquidity fell from USD 1,455.5 million at January 31, 2026 to USD 1,086.5 million at August 1, 2026 as acquisitions, a free cash outflow and share repurchases outweighed earnings, with the revolver undrawn and maturing in December 2030, so creditors have cushion but the next acquisition or buyback draws on it. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 19–21; EX-99.2_2026-08-26_q22027presentationmateri.htm.jsonl, page 4; calculation C03

- Customer concentration is the primary downside path. AT&T, Verizon and Lumen supplied 50.2% of fiscal 2026 revenues, agreements are terminable for convenience, and a program deferral worth about USD 150 million of wireless revenue already moved into fiscal 2028; an EBITDA fall of 39.24% on trailing earnings would take net debt to the 4.50x covenant maximum on an illustrative reported basis. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); EX-99.2_2026-08-26_q22027presentationmateri.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 21; calculation C01

runs.text: Strengths. Scale and visibility come first: contract revenues of USD 5,545.9 million, backlog of USD 12,242 million and multi-year agreements for 86.6% of revenues mean fixed work flows continue through a capital-budget wobble, which supports debt service. Second, the capital structure has been extended: secured term debt matures in 2030 and 2033, the revolver is undrawn and the first bullet maturity is the 2029 notes, so refinancing pressure is distant. Third, cash cover is wide: reported EBITDA covered cash interest 10.49x on trailing earnings. Fourth, the new Building Systems segment earns an adjusted margin of 21.10% and no cash dividend has been paid since 1982, which supports deleveraging if cash is retained. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 54–55; 10-K_2026-01-31_dy-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 46

Weaknesses. Customer concentration is first: three customers were 50.2% of fiscal 2026 revenues and can end agreements for convenience, so one capital decision moves earnings. Second, free cash flow is unstable, with conversion of 61.84% in fiscal 2026 and a first-half outflow in each of the last two years, because working capital absorbs cash; the supplier finance float of USD 367.4 million would add to that if withdrawn. Third, leverage has risen since January 2025 on acquisition debt while shares are repurchased and a further USD 150.0 million is authorised. Fourth, secured debt of USD 2,340.0 million ranks ahead of the notes and the new segment's customer base and controls are unproven. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 30; calculation C05

Financial profile by dimension. Scale and market position is Strong on revenue and national footprint, though market share is not supplied. Competitive advantage is Average because the industry is fragmented with few barriers to entry and agreements are awarded competitively. Business diversification is Weak on customers and Average on segments after the Building Systems acquisitions. Cost and capex flexibility is Average: customers supply most materials and fiscal 2027 net capital expenditure is guided near the fiscal 2026 level, but labor is the main cost. Margin stability is Average: adjusted margin rose to 13.3% in fiscal 2026 and 14.6% in the first half of fiscal 2027, yet management expects a slight Communications decline. Free cash flow stability is Weak. Ability to refinance is Average on recent bank execution, with ratings and prices not supplied. Liquidity position is Average, adequate but declining. Financial policy and governance is Average: no sponsor or dividend, but debt-funded acquisitions and buybacks. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2026-01-31_dy-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-K_2026-01-31_dy-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 72; EX-99.2_2026-08-26_q22027presentationmateri.htm.jsonl, page 5

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: Dycom completed the acquisition of Power Solutions on December 23, 2025 for a stated price of USD 1,950 million on a cash-free, debt-free basis, with total consideration later stated at USD 2,008.7 million after a working-capital adjustment. The consideration was USD 1,644.9 million of cash and 1,011,069 newly issued Dycom shares valued at USD 351.0 million, plus assumed seller debt of USD 64.8 million, so the buyer financed most of the price with new secured borrowing, and holders of the 2029 notes now rank behind USD 2,340.0 million of secured term loans that stood at USD 450.0 million a year earlier. Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_dy-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 50; 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2025-10-25_dy-20251025.htm.jsonl, page 25; calculation C05; calculation C09

The financing was reshaped between signing and closing. The November 2025 commitment letter offered a USD 1,000 million term loan A, a USD 700 million bridge and a USD 445 million backstop, but the executed structure on December 23, 2025 was a USD 1,540.0 million term loan A, a USD 800.0 million revolver and a USD 600.0 million bridge, and on January 27, 2026 a USD 800.0 million term loan B refinanced the bridge and added cash to the balance sheet. No bond was issued, the 4.50% notes due 2029 remain the only unsecured debt instrument listed, and the new facilities mature in 2030 and 2033, so refinancing risk moved out in time while secured debt moved ahead of the notes. Basis: 10-Q_2025-10-25_dy-20251025.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2026-01-31_dy-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 76; 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 18–21

The second acquisition, National Technology Integrators, was agreed on May 22, 2026 and closed on July 2, 2026 for total consideration of USD 271.4 million, mostly cash from balance sheet funds, with USD 45.0 million paid in shares and USD 12.3 million of seller debt assumed. It adds low-voltage and structured cabling work to Building Systems and, with the first acquisition, shows an acquisition cadence of two deals in seven months, the first funded by secured debt and the second by cash on hand, and neither by new bonds. Basis: 10-Q_2026-05-02_dy-20260502.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-08-01_dy-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11; EX-99.2_2026-05-27_q12027presentationmateri.htm.jsonl, page 5; calculation C06; calculation C09

fields.value: Leverage rose because acquisition debt arrived before the acquired earnings were fully in the base. Net debt on carrying values was 1.50x reported EBITDA at the January 2025 year end, 2.99x at the January 2026 year end and 2.73x on trailing earnings to August 1, 2026; total debt over reported EBITDA was 4.00x and 3.11x at the last two dates. The step from the January 2025 level came from borrowing for Power Solutions in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, and the fall since year end is earnings growth and the part-period inclusion of the acquired earnings, not debt reduction: debt was not repaid and a further acquisition was paid in cash. Neither ratio is a covenant ratio, and the reported covenant ratios are not printed.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Cash servicing looks strong but flatters the current debt load. Reported EBITDA covered cash interest paid 11.30x in fiscal 2026 and 10.49x on trailing earnings, yet trailing cash interest holds the acquisition debt for only part of the base year, cash interest paid in the first half of fiscal 2027 alone was nearly twice the first half of fiscal 2026, accrued net interest expense in the half exceeded cash paid by a margin shown in the definition conflict register, and interest payable on the balance sheet more than tripled, so cash interest will rise toward the accrual as it is paid. Cover on the issuer's adjusted EBITDA is higher still, at 11.10x, but the add-backs are the issuer's.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Cash-flow quality is seasonal and working-capital driven. Free cash flow was an outflow of USD 54.2 million in the first half of fiscal 2027 after receivables absorbed cash, although days sales outstanding improved to 101 days from 108 days a year earlier, and the supplier finance program, with USD 367.4 million of confirmed obligations inside accounts payable at August 1, 2026 against USD 226.4 million at year end, supplies part of the operating funding. If the program were withdrawn, payables would shorten and operating cash flow would absorb the difference before any change in earnings, so the float is working-capital funding that behaves like short-term borrowing and is not in the debt figure. Receivables sold without recourse under a customer-sponsored program also shorten collection, and their volume is not printed.

fields.value: Liquidity is adequate but fell. Liquidity of USD 1,086.5 million at August 1, 2026 compares with USD 1,455.5 million at the year end, a fall that follows cash paid for acquisitions, including USD 225.5 million in the second quarter, the first-half working-capital outflow and share repurchases; no revolver borrowing is outstanding and the revolver and Term Loan A mature on December 23, 2030, ahead of the 2033 Term Loan B. The 2029 notes are the first bullet maturity. The two maintenance covenants, a maximum net leverage ratio of 4.50 to 1.00 and a minimum interest cover of 2.50 to 1.00, are reported as met, but their headroom is not calculable from the printed figures.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The strongest contrary evidence is the pace of earnings growth: first-half adjusted EBITDA margin was 14.6% against 13.5% a year earlier, backlog reached USD 12,242 million at August 1, 2026, and the Building Systems segment reached a margin above the Communications segment. That supports a faster fall in leverage than the debt-only view, and would win if trailing earnings keep absorbing the acquired businesses while debt stays flat. It would lose if the deferral of wireless program revenue announced with the second quarter results widens or customer concentration, with AT&T and Verizon each above 10% of revenue, leads to capital expenditure cuts, because working capital would then absorb cash before earnings fell. The observable tests are receivable days, the supplier finance balance, accrued interest payable and the next two quarterly balance sheets.

fields.value: Data and definition risks bound these conclusions. Reported EBITDA is derived and includes other income and the loss on debt extinguishment, adjusted EBITDA is the issuer's, fiscal 2026 has 53 weeks, both purchase price allocations are preliminary, the balance sheet at the end of the first half of fiscal 2026 is not supplied, and gross interest, restricted cash and the amount of receivables sold are not separately established. Operating lease liabilities, performance and surety bonds and the supplier finance float lie outside the debt figure, so total claims on cash flow are larger than the leverage ratios show.

fields.value: Business and governance review of DYCOM INDUSTRIES INC as of 2026-11-05 under the credit_snapshot pathway. Scope is the business model, customers, ownership and control, governance, acquisitions and financing events, and capital allocation, from the filings and presentations supplied up to the quarter ended August 1, 2026.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: No external sources were used. Dates identify the signature or cover dates the documents state.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Dycom is a concentrated, contract-based telecom construction business now widening into data-center electrical work, and its debt-funded acquisitions and share repurchases, not any controlling holder, are the governance risk creditors should watch.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Three customers supplied 50.2% of fiscal 2026 contract revenues, yet 86.6% of revenues came from multi-year master service agreements and backlog reached USD 12,242 million at August 1, 2026, so visibility is good but not committed. No controlling holder or sponsor is disclosed, and the proxy statement that would show holders above 5% is not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Customer concentration is the dominant business risk. AT&T, Verizon and Lumen supplied 50.2% of fiscal 2026 contract revenues, and AT&T and Verizon alone supplied 31.8% of first-half fiscal 2027 revenues, so one customer's capital budget can move earnings and receivables quickly. Agreements are generally terminable for convenience and customers are not committed to specific volumes, so backlog measures awarded work rather than guaranteed work. Wireless program revenue that management defers into fiscal 2028 shows how timing, not demand, can break the quarter.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Contract structure gives revenue visibility but limited price protection. Multi-year master service agreements were 86.6% of fiscal 2026 revenues against 79.3% a year earlier, and next-twelve-month backlog is 52.87% of total backlog. Work is priced by unit with discrete task pricing, and management states that it may be unable to pass labor and training cost increases to customers, so margin, not volume, is the exposed line when costs rise.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Acquisitions have changed the business mix faster than the track record supports. Building Systems supplied 20.0% of first-half fiscal 2027 revenues at an adjusted EBITDA margin of 21.10% against 12.92% in Communications, but it rests on one large acquisition completed on December 23, 2025 and a second on July 2, 2026, and goodwill and intangible assets are now 38.75% of total assets. The new customers are described as highly concentrated hyperscaler and data-center names, internal controls over the first acquisition were excluded from the annual assessment, and purchase accounting is preliminary, so margins and customer durability in the new segment are not yet proven through a cycle.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Governance risk is medium, driven by financial policy rather than control. No sponsor or controlling holder is disclosed, the company has paid no cash dividend since 1982 and intends to retain earnings, and the audit opinions and internal control opinion are unqualified. Against that, management is funding acquisitions with secured term debt and issued shares, repurchased shares in each of the last three fiscal periods, and on August 26, 2026 authorised a further USD 150.0 million repurchase program while carrying debt is about three times its January 2025 level, so shareholder returns compete with deleveraging.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Working-capital funding behaves like debt but sits outside it. A third-party supplier finance program was introduced in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 and held USD 367.4 million of confirmed obligations at August 1, 2026, and the company also sells receivables without recourse for one customer. Seasonal outdoor work leaves the January and April quarters weakest, so withdrawal of either arrangement would show first in operating cash flow.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The strongest evidence against a cautious view is the combination of record backlog of USD 12,242 million, organic revenue growth of 16.7% in the second quarter, management's statement that customers are extending contract durations, and a Building Systems margin well above Communications. If those hold while debt stays flat, trailing earnings absorb the acquisitions and the concentration risk is outweighed by contracted visibility. The view would turn more negative if a top-three customer cut or deferred a large program beyond the wireless deferral already announced, if further debt-funded acquisitions or repurchases were made before leverage fell, if the shares issued to the Power Solutions seller were sold in size, or if the new segment's margin fell back toward the Communications level. A proxy statement showing a holder above 5% or board changes could also move the control and governance view in either direction.

fields.value: Strengths. Scale and visibility come first: contract revenues of USD 5,545.9 million, backlog of USD 12,242 million and multi-year agreements for 86.6% of revenues mean fixed work flows continue through a capital-budget wobble, which supports debt service. Second, the capital structure has been extended: secured term debt matures in 2030 and 2033, the revolver is undrawn and the first bullet maturity is the 2029 notes, so refinancing pressure is distant. Third, cash cover is wide: reported EBITDA covered cash interest 10.49x on trailing earnings. Fourth, the new Building Systems segment earns an adjusted margin of 21.10% and no cash dividend has been paid since 1982, which supports deleveraging if cash is retained.

Third, leverage has risen since January 2025 on acquisition debt while shares are repurchased and a further USD 150.0 million is authorised. Fourth, secured debt of USD 2,340.0 million ranks ahead of the notes and the new segment's customer base and controls are unproven.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Dycom is a United States specialty contractor to telephone companies, cable operators, wireless carriers and utilities, with a Building Systems segment for data-center electrical work since December 23, 2025. It is publicly listed with no sponsor or controlling holder disclosed, so financial policy is set by management rather than an equity owner, and creditors cannot rely on sponsor support or fear sponsor extraction; the missing proxy statement leaves holders above 5% open. The debt sits at the parent with guarantees from substantially all domestic subsidiaries, so the structure is flat and structural subordination is limited to non-guarantor subsidiaries not identified in the filings.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Demand follows telecommunications and data-center capital budgets, with fiber-to-the-home, long-haul fiber and wireless programs the stated drivers. Work is priced per unit under master service agreements awarded competitively, with customers able to terminate for convenience, so revenue is recurring and visible but not committed and pricing power is limited. The risk mechanism is a customer cutting or deferring a program, as the wireless deferral shows, which lowers billable volume faster than Dycom can resize labor; the implication for creditors is volatile earnings around a large backlog rather than structural decline.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Labor and subcontractors are the main costs, customers supply most materials, and tasks are priced per unit, so management states it may be unable to pass labor and training cost increases to customers. Margins can be defended under moderate volume pressure through subcontractor flexing, but operating leverage works both ways: the group adjusted margin rose to 14.6% in the first half of fiscal 2027 on volume and mix, while the Communications margin fell in the second quarter to 13.6% from 14.9%. The implication is that margin, not volume, is the first line to give under wage inflation or a program loss.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Capital expenditure is mainly fleet replacement and growth, with a fiscal 2027 net outlay guided at USD 210.0 million to USD 220.0 million, so it can be flexed in a downturn. Free cash flow conversion has swung from 24.28% in fiscal 2025 to 61.84% in fiscal 2026 and turned negative in each first half, because receivables and seasonality absorb cash in the January and April quarters. Cash interest, cash taxes and acquisition spending then compete for what remains, so EBITDA translates into durable free cash flow only across the full year and only if working capital normalises. Operating lease liabilities of USD 228.725 million and performance and surety bonds of USD 1,215.8 million lie outside the debt figure, so claims on cash flow are larger than the leverage ratios show.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Rivalry is high in a fragmented industry with few barriers to entry and some customers self-performing work, which limits pricing and keeps agreements competitively bid. Buyer power is strong because three customers hold half of revenue and can terminate for convenience; supplier power is low because customers supply most materials and subcontractors are small, though skilled labor is the binding input. Substitution through network technology change is a long-dated risk. Policy matters through state and federal broadband spending, which management cites as a demand driver; this is a tailwind to volume but not a credit protection. The credit translation is that bargaining power sits with customers, so margin protection depends on execution rather than market structure.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Over the next 12 to 24 months management has raised its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook to USD 7.48 billion to USD 7.66 billion, with Communications now expecting a slight margin decline because of the wireless deferral and Building Systems a high-teens to low-twenties margin. These are non-GAAP management expectations and are not reconciled to reported results. Tailwinds are record backlog, customers extending contract durations and data-center electrical demand; headwinds are customer program timing, labor cost, integration of two acquisitions and the seasonally weak cash profile of the quarters ending in January and April. Over three to five years, fiber and data-center build programmes support volume, but concentration and acquisition-funded leverage remain the credit constraints.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The initiating event is a top customer deferring or cutting a large fiber or wireless program, as the wireless deferral already shows on a small scale. The first operational break is lower billable work in Communications against a largely fixed local labor base, so margin falls before revenue. EBITDA then declines, receivables days rise from 101 days toward the 108 days of a year earlier while the supplier finance float may shorten, and free cash flow turns negative. On reported EBITDA, trailing earnings would have to fall by 39.24% before carrying-basis net debt reached the 4.50x covenant maximum, and cash interest cover would stay above 2.50x until trailing EBITDA fell 76.17%; both are illustrative and not covenant tests. Liquidity of USD 1,086.5 million, an undrawn revolver and discretionary capital expenditure and buybacks are the management levers, so resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress in a single-program shock, while a simultaneous loss of two large customers combined with further acquisitions is not tested here.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Overall, Dycom presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, multi-year contracts and record backlog, but credit quality is constrained by customer concentration, acquisition-funded leverage and weak free cash flow stability. Cash-flow durability appears adequate over a full year but weak within it, because working capital absorbs cash seasonally. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on continued earnings growth and bank-market access, since the first bullet maturity is the April 2029 notes and the secured term loans mature in 2030 and 2033. The primary downside path is a top-customer program cut reaching margin and then working capital while debt stays at its acquisition level. Further analysis would require covenant calculations, pro forma earnings and market data. Credit assessment complete. Top risk: customer concentration.
